# Apple Watch vs WHOOP: Here’s what I learned after 60 days wearing both [Video]

[[image: Avatar for Fernando Silva | https://secure.gravatar.com/avatar/51c53e5c5859bfaa0037d265388173f156f15457a06350a060dac70848e4db4a?s=30&d=mm&r=r] -> https://9to5mac.com/author/fernandosilva/]
[Fernando Silva -> https://9to5mac.com/author/fernandosilva/] | May 8 2026 - 8:40 am PT

20 Comments

[image: | https://9to5mac.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/6/2026/05/fernando.jpg?quality=82&strip=all&w=1600]

For the last 60 days, I have been wearing an [Apple Watch Ultra 2 -> https://amzn.to/4nhBYjj] and the latest [WHOOP MG. -> https://amzn.to/4tZDaKL]I wanted to better understand the hype surrounding WHOOP. If you spend enough time online, you can see that WHOOP users are loud and proud. It’s marketed as a serious wellness and fitness tracker that high-profile athletes and Silicon Valley tech founders wear. So, as someone who cares about their fitness, wellness, sleep, and overall health, I felt like I had to experience this for myself and, of course, compare it to the fitness tracker that I have been wearing for well over a decade: the [Apple Watch -> https://amzn.to/4uBhowC]. This is what I learned after 60 days.

Be sure to watch our in-depth video review below. We go hands-on with both of them for over 60 days and learn a lot about what they each can and cannot do.

## Completely different design philosophies

The first thing I noticed when I finally got my WHOOP set up is that these fitness trackers are built around completely different ideas. The WHOOP has no screen. It’s lightweight at just 26.5g, low-profile, and designed to disappear on your body. I wore it on my right wrist, but you can wear it on your bicep or even on your waistband with the correct accessory. There is nearly nothing to interact with. You put it on and let it collect your data in the background. And that is the point, it’s meant to feel passive.

Then you have the [Apple Watch -> https://amzn.to/4uBhowC], and it’s the complete opposite. In my testing, I used the [Apple Watch Ultra 2 -> https://amzn.to/4nhBYjj], but everything I mention applies to any [Apple Watch. -> https://amzn.to/4uBhowC] The Apple Watch is a smartwatch first; an extension of your iPhone on your wrist. It has a bright display, tactile buttons, apps, notifications, and can make phone calls, doing pretty much everything your iPhone does at a smaller scale.

[image: | https://9to5mac.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/6/2026/05/AW-vs-WHOOP.jpg?quality=82&strip=all&w=1024]

[image: | https://9to5mac.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/6/2026/05/AW-vs-WHOOP-6.jpg?quality=82&strip=all&w=1024]

[image: | https://9to5mac.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/6/2026/05/AW-vs-WHOOP-7.jpg?quality=82&strip=all&w=1024]

Even though I’m comparing these from a health and fitness perspective, the [Apple Watch -> https://amzn.to/4uBhowC] still feels like a tool you actively use throughout the day, while the WHOOP feels more like something you forget is even there. I understand the appeal of an accessory that is intentional, hyper-focused on one thing, and also distraction-free. I did enjoy that aspect of it. The only time I physically interacted with the WHOOP was to charge it. So if you are deciding between the two and want to be dead set on it being a fitness tracker, then the WHOOP will do that for you.

## Battery life

The WHOOP’s distraction-free nature results in amazing battery life. It is rated for about 14 days of battery life, and I consistently got around 10–12 days with the [WHOOP MG -> https://amzn.to/4tZDaKL]before needing to charge it. The charging system is also pretty clever because, in a perfect world, WHOOP does not want you to take the device off at all. So the charger is actually a battery pack that can be slipped onto the WHOOP to charge it, even while you are wearing it. I personally did not do that; I preferred to take it off while charging, but it is a nice aspect of the charging system. But that constant data collection is a huge part of the WHOOP philosophy.

[image: | https://9to5mac.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/6/2026/05/AW-vs-WHOOP-9.jpg?quality=82&strip=all&w=1024]

[image: | https://9to5mac.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/6/2026/05/AW-vs-WHOOP-8-edited.jpg?quality=82&strip=all]

Then you have the [Apple Watch -> https://amzn.to/4uBhowC]. Again, I am using my 2-year-old Apple [Watch Ultra 2 -> https://amzn.to/4nhBYjj]. At its best, the Apple Watch is rated for 36 hours and has a low-power mode that extends that to 60 hours. But since it is 2 years old, I get about 30-32 hours of battery life on it before I need to charge it. I usually charge it daily when I am in the shower or doing dishes. Battery is something I think about constantly with my Apple Watch. And if you work out for hours at a time, multiple times a day, it will drain even faster. It’s safe to assume that you will easily get through a day on one charge, but you will need to charge it on day 2.

If your number one priority is uninterrupted 24/7 tracking, WHOOP absolutely has the edge here.

## The health sensors situation

This one actually surprised me. Going into this comparison, I assumed the WHOOP would have every advanced health sensor imaginable. But in reality, the Apple Watch actually has more sensors than the [WHOOP MG. -> https://amzn.to/4tZDaKL]

Apple Watch sensors:

- Optical heart rate sensor

- Electrical heart sensor for ECG

- Blood oxygen sensor

- Skin temperature sensor

- Accelerometer

- Gyroscope

- Dual-frequency GPS (or single band on regular Apple Watch)

- Altimeter

- Compass

- Ambient light sensor

- Depth gauge

- Water temperature sensor

Meanwhile, the WHOOP MG has:

- PPG heart rate sensor

- Heart rate variability tracking

- Skin temperature tracking

- Accelerometer for movement and sleep

[image: | https://9to5mac.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/6/2026/05/AW-vs-WHOOP-10.jpg?quality=82&strip=all&w=1024]

Technically, the [WHOOP MG -> https://amzn.to/4tZDaKL] also advertises blood pressure tracking, but to set it up there is a lot of friction, and the feature feels half-baked.

The interesting part is that even though the Apple Watch is doing more overall, the core fitness and recovery data between the two is very comparable. The heart rate tracking, sleep tracking, and recovery metrics are all presented with mostly the same values. The difference comes down to how the data is presented to us.

## The app experience

Now this is WHOOP’s bread and butter. The WHOOP app experience is actually great. You get recovery scores, strain targets, sleep coaching, and an overall experience focused on proactivity. So instead of just showing you the data, it wants to guide the interpretation of that data and help you take action to improve your wellness. In their most recent update, they also added an AI assistant, which I really like. You can simply ask questions like:

- Should I work out today?

- Did I recover enough for a run?

- Why did I sleep poorly?

- Should I focus on recovery today?

Then, based on your WHOOP health data, it will guide you to the best action plan for that moment or day.

[image: | https://9to5mac.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/6/2026/05/AW-vs-WHOOP-11.jpg?quality=82&strip=all&w=1024]

[image: | https://9to5mac.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/6/2026/05/AW-vs-WHOOP-12.jpg?quality=82&strip=all&w=1024]

[image: | https://9to5mac.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/6/2026/05/AW-vs-WHOOP-14.jpg?quality=82&strip=all&w=1024]

The Apple Health app is the opposite. Apple gives you all the raw data, but it’s mostly up to you to interpret what that all means. You can view a lot of the same metrics like HRV, VO2 Max, resting heart rate, and everything else, but Apple doesn’t help you put an action plan together to help you improve it. There are some explanations and blurbs that tell you what HRV is and what it means to have it high or low, but it won’t take your HRV data and tell you how to improve it.

Personally, I think that when it comes to tracking all of your health and fitness metrics, most people want guidance on what to do with this data. So, because of that, I would give the edge to the WHOOP app. It’s clean, easy to navigate, and helps you proactively make tangible improvements to your health, while the [Apple Watch -> https://amzn.to/4uBhowC] takes a more “figure it out yourself” approach.

## WHOOP’s issue

Coming into this experience, I thought the hardware was what set the WHOOP apart from the rest. But I quickly learned that the Apple Watch offers far more sensors and health-related hardware. Then I started playing with the WHOOP app, and it seemed the app was the actual differentiator for them. The software layer on top of the WHOOP was what really set them apart, so I thought.

Then I found the app called [Bevel -> https://apple.co/42nXIAw]. This app essentially turns any modern Apple Watch into a WHOOP. [Bevel -> https://apple.co/42nXIAw] has everything WHOOP has: recovery scores, sleep analysis, strain tracking, and AI-based insights. It even has a similar conversational AI layer that helps interpret your data just as WHOOP does. When I found the [Bevel -> https://apple.co/42nXIAw] app, things just clicked in my mind. I realized I did not need the WHOOP hardware at all.

[image: | https://9to5mac.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/6/2026/05/AW-vs-WHOOP-13.jpg?quality=82&strip=all&w=1024]

[image: | https://9to5mac.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/6/2026/05/AW-vs-WHOOP-15.jpg?quality=82&strip=all&w=1024]

What WHOOP really opened my eyes to was third-party health app ecosystems on the Apple Watch. For over a decade, I had relied on Apple’s default fitness and health apps, but there are hundreds (maybe thousands) of apps that build on Apple Watch data in interesting ways. [Bevel -> https://apple.co/42nXIAw] was just the one who felt closest to the WHOOP. So if you combine this new realization with WHOOP’s price point and subscription model, it really changes how you view and justify the WHOOP. Especially if you already have an Apple Watch.

## The pricing and subscription situation

This is where things get interesting for my comparison. The WHOOP MG costs $359. They have two cheaper options with the ONE starting at $199 and the PEAK starting at $239. But I wanted to test their best version, so I went with the WHOOP MG LIFE at $359. For that price, you get the WHOOP, the fabric band, and a battery pack that doubles as a charger. But what baffles me is that the $359 price is PER YEAR. You can literally get a brand new [Apple Watch Series 11 from Amazon for $299 -> https://amzn.to/4uBhowC]. So you could technically buy a brand-new watch every year for less than the price of a WHOOP MG subscription.

Then, as I mentioned above, I realized that what you are paying for is the app experience. The WHOOP hardware itself is not particularly special and does not have any proprietary features. Meanwhile, apps like Bevel cost significantly less. So if you already own an [Apple Watch -> https://amzn.to/4uBhowC], it becomes very difficult to justify the long-term cost of a WHOOP.

## What makes [WHOOP -> https://amzn.to/4tZDaKL] special

But, even with everything I mentioned above, I can still see the appeal of the WHOOP. There was something refreshing about wearing a device with no screen. There were no notifications, no distractions, no phantom buzzing; it was purely built for health and recovery. I 100% see that there is a growing audience of people who are tired of having another smart device attached to them all day. People want to track their data, but also wear a normal watch that doesn’t have a flashing screen. So the WHOOP’s intentionality is actually refreshing.

There also seems to be an aura around WHOOP. They have a great marketing team and fantastic branding. Athletes wear it, tech founders and tech bros love it, and high performers are drawn to it. The WHOOP has an exclusivity feeling around it that reminds me of the early days of the Apple Watch. But after living with it for over two months, the experience really did not live up to that aura, for me.

[image: | https://9to5mac.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/6/2026/05/AW-vs-WHOOP-4.jpg?quality=82&strip=all&w=1024]

[image: | https://9to5mac.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/6/2026/05/AW-vs-WHOOP-5.jpg?quality=82&strip=all&w=1024]

There were a few annoying nuances that a $359 priced product should not have. For example, I rely heavily on my [Apple Watch -> https://amzn.to/4uBhowC]to slowly wake me up with its haptic engine. I love it. The WHOOP also has a vibration motor, but it’s terrible. It feels like something that should be on a $20 device, not a nearly $400 device. The way you turn off the vibration alarm is also clunky. You are supposed to double-tap the device, and it literally never works. I have to slap my wrist 10 times for the vibration to stop. And then the fabric band stinks, literally. Since its fabric, the sweat and moisture stick to it, and over time, it gets very nasty very quickly. They should have gone with a rubber band for the default option.

## Top comment by The Phone Guy

Liked by 12 people

I looked at whoop but decided I would never give up my Apple Watch and didn't want to wear multiple devices. Once I started using Bevel two months ago it has changed my life. I have lost weight and are more mindful of nutrition and activity. **One thing to note is the subscription is 100% optional and Bevel is free otherwise.

View all comments

Those little things add up over time when it’s a product you’re supposed to wear 24/7 and is marketed as premium and high-quality.

## Final thoughts

After this comparison period, I did learn who the WHOOP was for. If you want great battery life, no distractions, passive wellness tracking, and a more guided health experience, then I get the appeal. But it still baffles me that it doesn’t feel premium and lacks GPS. I feel like everyone is now into running, so the fact that you cannot track runs with GPS is wild to me.

But for me personally, it’s not enough to pull me away from the Apple Watch. Especially once I realized that the Apple Watch can basically give you all the advantages the WHOOP has through third-party apps like [Bevel -> https://apple.co/42nXIAw], and the [Apple Watch Series 11 -> https://amzn.to/4uBhowC] is cheaper than the [WHOOP MG -> https://amzn.to/4tZDaKL] and does way more. And for those who want a distraction-free experience, you can still do that on your Apple Watch by turning off a few settings. So for that reason, I would recommend an Apple Watch to 9 out of 10 people.

Because at the end of the day, the Apple Watch can be a WHOOP, but the WHOOP can never be an Apple Watch.

# Apple Watch vs. Whoop Band: Here's Which Wearable to Buy (CNET)

Source URL: https://www.cnet.com/tech/mobile/apple-watch-vs-whoop-band-buying-guide/ (canonical, confirmed from page)
Publisher: CNET. Byline: Vanessa Hand Orellana, Principal Writer. Published 2026-04-17 (datePublished and dateModified 2026-04-17T12:00:00-04:00 in page metadata).
Captured: 2026-11-20 via curl (browser User-Agent, HTTP 200, 335,076 bytes) and deterministic stdlib HTML extraction of the page's <article> element. Headings, paragraphs, the subscription table (cells prefixed "|"), photo captions, in-article links (shown as [anchor -> URL]) and image references kept. Navigation, the H1 block outside <article>, related-story rails and footer omitted.
Observed ranking: position 5 for "whoop vs apple watch" (Ahrefs SERP overview, US, update 2026-11-17, orchestrator-supplied); cited by the AI Overview. Hands-on first-person comparison (Apple Watch Series 11 and Whoop MG, two months). Affiliate links.

---

[image: vswhoop | https://www.cnet.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/0b2d4a6d-b987-488d-82e0-d1e83e77893e.jpg?fit=1200,675]

The Apple Watch (top) and the Whoop Band (bottom) on my 6-inch wrist. 

Vanessa Hand Orellana/CNET

The [Whoop band -> https://www.cnet.com/health/fitness/whoop-5-0-review/] has been on my radar for six years before finally testing it out for myself. It’s a screenless fitness tracker built for serious athletes, and the sheer volume of training metrics always felt a little intimidating to me as a mere mortal.

The [Apple Watch -> https://www.cnet.com/tech/mobile/best-apple-watch/], on the other hand, is like that approachable friend who speaks to you on your level — much more my speed, six years ago.

But after seeing how many Whoop owners love the band, it was time to confront what intimidated me and see if it could outperform my Apple Watch Series 11. Two months later, the Whoop has transformed the way I work out and surfaced insights about my own body that weren’t on my radar before. Don’t mistake this for a breakup story — I’m not ditching my Apple Watch, yet.

The wearable space is evolving rapidly, with AI opening up the possibility of finally turning years’ worth of raw health and fitness data into actual advice. The [standout smartwatches -> https://www.cnet.com/tech/mobile/best-smartwatch/] and trackers are now built around AI health coaches, proactive longevity features and metrics that respond visibly when you make the right changes. 

As wearable sensors become more capable and health information gets more complex, the stakes are higher. It’s more important than ever to understand what each device does and which one will give you the most relevant information. That’s why just comparing specs won’t cut it. To make this personal, I had to literally become a test subject and wear both the Whoop MG band and my [Apple Watch Series 11 -> https://www.cnet.com/tech/mobile/apple-watch-series-11-is-still-my-goldilocks-pick-but-not-by-much/] long enough to unlock every single feature. 

Comparing the Whoop band to an Apple Watch is like comparing a motorcycle to a minivan. They’re two different beasts that just happen to drive on the same street (your wrist). Health tracking is the main event for the Whoop, and likely the reason you’re considering it, whereas on the Apple Watch, it’s just one of the items on the menu. In an ideal world, you’d get both, but for this comparison, I’ll focus on the health features. 

[Apple Watch Series 11 -> https://cc.cnet.com/v1/otc/04Yxjj1rHOmYAxbnVDhvKNn?merchant=00ebVEnjbokXgtzpToBWfNz&url=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.target.com%2Fp%2Fapple-watch-series-11%2F-%2FA-94966472&u=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.cnet.com%2Ftech%2Fmobile%2Fapple-watch-vs-whoop-band-buying-guide%2F]

[Whoop MG Life -> https://cc.cnet.com/v1/otc/04Yxjj1rHOmYAxbnVDhvKNn?merchant=07ceq7iAfFfRlRYt8DCvPYM&url=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.bestbuy.com%2Fproduct%2Fwhoop-mg-life-health-and-fitness-tracker-12-month-membership-obsidian-titanium-2025%2FJ3GW3TK8G7&u=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.cnet.com%2Ftech%2Fmobile%2Fapple-watch-vs-whoop-band-buying-guide%2F]

## The price to play

The Whoop has two immediate red flags for me. WTF is this name? I’ve never answered so many “the what?” questions when asked what’s on my wrist. But that’s a superficial me-problem.

On the surface, the Apple Watch Series 11 costs more: $400 for the 42mm Wi-Fi model. The Whoop MG is $360. But that’s not a one-time payment. The Whoop band itself is just a bonus; what you’re really paying for is a subscription model that ranges from $199-359 yearly. The plan’s price determines which band model you get and what metrics you unlock. 

## Whoop subscription plans

| Plan name | Band included | Price per year | Battery life | Key features

| One | Whoop 4.0 | $199 | 5 days | Core metrics: vitals and training scores

| Peak | Whoop 5.0 | $239 | 14 days | Adds aging insights (Healthspan)

| Life | Whoop MG | $359 | 14 days | Adds ECG and AFib detection

Not everyone’s willing to commit to yet another subscription, and if you’re in it for the long haul, you could end up spending more than the cost of the Apple Watch. But the bigger filter might be compatibility: The Whoop is the only device compatible with both iOS and Android. The Apple Watch is locked to the iPhone only. 

## First impressions and a Whoop thong?!

The fact that I’d never worn a Whoop band before gives the Apple Watch an unfair advantage, especially since it has a screen; the Whoop doesn’t. I’m used to glancing down at my wrist for a time check, so seeing something occupy space on my wrist that didn’t tell time was genuinely infuriating. 

Whereas the Whoop doesn’t present any data on the actual band, the Apple Watch shows you the time, weather forecast, tides, stock price and more. You control which notifications you receive, but it demands your attention throughout the day, from stand reminders to Slack alerts. You can also use it as a wallet or a camera remote, making it more like a mini version of your iPhone that just happens to be watching out for your health.

[image: whoop | https://www.cnet.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/73bc2b03-9b32-42a6-a610-710094be422e.jpg?fit=1200,675]

The Whoop MG with the proprietary band (left) and the third party alternative (right).

Vanessa Hand Orellana/CNET

I can see the Whoop’s lack of screen as an asset for minimalists who don’t want the noise. While it was easy to forget I was wearing it, the band doesn’t exactly fade into the background like a [smart ring -> https://www.cnet.com/health/fitness/best-smart-ring-oura-ring/] does. The Whoop’s sensor alone is almost the size of the Apple Watch’s screen, but has a thicker profile, which makes it bulkier when wearing to bed.

You can also camouflage the device more easily since the band sits over the sensor. Whoop offers a range of clasp and band materials, and even a [$20 third-party starlight gray band -> https://a.co/d/084WssCU] made it feel more subtle on my wrist than the original black. The Apple Watch also has a wide selection of bands, but the screen is always front and center.

[image: screenshot-2026-04-14-at-11-29-13am.png | https://www.cnet.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/166834e7-332d-4656-b639-df3681d924d3.png?fit=1200,675]

You can’t make this up: Whoop is thong-compatible.

Whoop

The Apple Watch is also mostly relegated to the wrist. The Whoop is more versatile in that it can take readings from different parts of your body, including your chest and lower back. That can be useful for athletes who can’t wear anything on their limbs or for amputees. Whoop even sells garments to hold the sensor in place, including a [thong -> https://shop.whoop.com/us/en/products/essential-thong/], though I still can’t wrap my mind around wearing any device below the belt; I’m clearly not the target audience. The only alternative I’d realistically use is the arm or bicep band for sleep.

Suffice to say, you won’t get that range of wear with the Apple Watch.

[image: I Ran 30 Miles and THIS Is the Most Accurate Smartwatch | https://cdn.ex.co/transformations-account/production/bf6379df-047b-4e0a-b804-89ce1cc89281/40d3d31d-bae3-4359-a8ec-24f7f275bef0/thumbnail-1080.webp]

## Similar metrics, different execution 

The Whoop is built for long-term data analysis, so saying the band’s tracking strategy was a slow burn is an understatement. It takes at least a week to unlock most metrics, and two weeks of 24/7 wear to see the rest. The Apple Watch has real-time metrics that you can start using as soon as you strap it on.

Even once you unlock the data, the Whoop always uses your phone as the middleman to deliver it. But the app earns its keep by nudging you (via notifications) whenever a new metric is unlocked, or if something needs your attention. The Apple Watch also notifies you of trends in the iPhone’s Health app, but those nudges are less frequent, so I end up forgetting to look. 

After two weeks of wear, the Whoop finally paid off

On the surface, the Apple Watch and Whoop measure similar biomarkers: heart rate, VO2 max, temperature, sleep and menstrual cycle. The difference is in what they do with that data. Apple gives you the numbers and some light guidance, but mostly leaves the interpretation up to you. Whoop collects the data and runs it through a single lens: How does this affect your training?

Sleep, heart rate and even your menstrual cycle phase get translated into a daily recovery score (how ready your body is to perform). Paired with a strain meter that tracks how hard you’ve pushed yourself, Whoop turns abstract data into a directive. On high-recovery, low-strain days, it pushes me to go harder. But the realities of parenting and work schedules don’t always align with my recovery score, and no amount of nudges can help me with that. There were times when a low recovery score convinced me I was too depleted for a hard workout (even though I could probably have pushed through). On other days, the score looked good, but my body was screaming the opposite.

The Apple Watch’s training load score measures workout effort, but it doesn’t tell you what to do with that info. It’s largely self-reported. Unlike the Whoop, which puts the strain score front and center in the app, Apple Watch training load trends are somewhat hidden in workout pages, so I don’t often remember to use it as guidance. 

[image: The Whoop Healthspan feature. | https://www.cnet.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/a3220dff-d0b1-4de3-b94e-77ccda44ebf5.jpg?fit=768,432]

Whoop’s Healthspan tab turns your vitals into aging insights, including a calculated “Whoop Age.”

Whoop

Both devices also track long-term trends such as VO2 max, or the measure of how efficient your body is at delivering oxygen to your muscles (a good indicator of cardiovascular health). Apple calls it Cardio Fitness score and surfaces it in the Health app. Whoop uses this metric (and other biomarkers) to calculate your “Whoop age,” how old your heart appears to be relative to your actual age, as well as your rate of aging. Not exactly a scientific term, but the effect is genius. Vanity and pride will get you invested in this number fast (at least it did for me).  

## Whoop’s health coach actually gets it 

The shining star, though, is the Whoop AI coach. As a certified [AI health coach skeptic -> https://www.cnet.com/tech/mobile/ai-health-coaches-the-next-frontier-in-wearables-or-privacy-nightmare/], I never thought I’d be praising one, but here we are. The key is that it doesn’t require you to interact with it; Whoop AI just pops up on its own when it has something important to flag in the app or when you summon it. Two days before my period, it warned me that workouts might feel harder because of hormonal changes (spot on) and gave me concrete workout alternatives for those days when my recovery was low. 

After an all-out 5K run, Whoop’s AI coach told me to take it easy for the next few days and not to push myself that hard more than once a week. In my black-and-white brain (before using the Whoop), every workout had to be all-out or it was simply not worth it. The coach pointed out that repeatedly spiking at peak heart rate might be working against my training. I did some non-AI-aided research myself and confirmed the AI coach was right. While raising your heart rate to peak occasionally can train your heart, sustained effort at this level increases your risk of injury. 

The AI coach also adjusted my recommended bedtime based on strain, prior sleep debt (accumulation of sleep deprivation) and nightly patterns to optimize recovery. I don’t follow it most days, but the fact that it’s personalized and dynamic makes me less likely to ignore it than just the Apple Watch’s static bedtime reminder. 

The closest Apple equivalent to Whoop’s AI coach is [Workout Buddy -> https://www.cnet.com/tech/mobile/i-underestimated-workout-buddy-apples-playing-the-long-game-for-ai-coaching/], an in-ear trainer that motivates you in real time and contextualizes your effort against your data history. For runners like me, that kind of screen-free guidance is essential and it’s where the Apple Watch pulls ahead. I rely on heart rate zones, pace and distance cues in real time, and without a screen or in-ear guidance, there’s no way to do the same on the Whoop. I can surface live stats and strain in the Whoop app, but that still means staring at my phone when I should be watching the trail in front of me. Even Whoop’s workout summaries don’t include variables such as distance or pace. 

Where Whoop holds its own is workout detection. Other screen-free wearables tend to miss lower-intensity sessions, but Whoop’s auto-detection has been spot on. The Apple Watch can detect some workouts automatically, but it’s less consistent and I usually end up starting them myself.

## The CNET accuracy test 

It’s one thing for these wearables to nail translating workouts into data, but now I had to make sure that data was accurate. I’ve run multiple accuracy tests on the Apple Watch, including a recent [30-mile cross-device testing blitz -> https://www.cnet.com/tech/mobile/i-ran-30-miles-testing-5-smartwatches-to-find-out-which-ones-you-can-actually-trust/] where it scored highest in heart rate tracking against five other smartwatches, outpacing even a Garmin watch.

I ran (literally) the same test on the Whoop using the Polar H10 chest strap for heart rate control.

[image: polar | https://www.cnet.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/52d50945-351c-4607-98c0-d5b6c37725d7.jpg?fit=1200,675]

The maximum and average heart rate from the Whoop was only two beats per minute off from the Polar chest strap during my test. 

Vanessa Hand Orellana/CNET

After three miles, the workout summary showed accurate results. It was only two beats below my peak heart rate (179 Whoop vs. 181 Polar), and two beats below my average HR. Workout summaries only tell part of the story, missing all the peaks and valleys that happen in between. That’s why I prefer to dig into the raw data. Polar makes it easy to export the second-by-second HR data into a spreadsheet, but getting that data off the Whoop app proved impossible. Even if there happens to be a workaround, it will likely require sleuth-level digging. For an athlete-focused wearable, that was extremely disappointing. Getting your heart rate data off the Apple Watch isn’t easy, but it is possible either by downloading your entire history or (as I’d recommend) downloading [this third-party app -> https://cc.cnet.com/v1/otc/04Yxjj1rHOmYAxbnVDhvKNn?url=https%3A%2F%2Fapps.apple.com%2Fus%2Fapp%2Fhealthfit%2Fid1202650514&u=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.cnet.com%2Ftech%2Fmobile%2Fapple-watch-vs-whoop-band-buying-guide%2F].

## Health and safety features

For all the fancy metrics and AI coaching, the Apple Watch still pulls ahead on raw health and safety features. Both devices have an ECG feature and AFib detection, though on the Whoop, you’re paying for the top-tier Life membership to get them. The Apple Watch has [FDA-cleared hypertension -> https://www.cnet.com/tech/mobile/the-fda-clears-the-apple-watch-for-hypertension-alerts/] alerts that flag signs of high blood pressure, sleep apnea detection and high and low heart-rate alerts. The Whoop can also give blood pressure estimates, but that first has to be calibrated with a traditional cuff and is intended only as a wellness feature (it’s not clinically validated).  

[image: apple watch 10 | https://www.cnet.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/80025a41-d644-48e2-b46b-e9b8348f37d5.png?fit=1200,675]

The Apple Watch can send out a cry for help if it auto detects a crash or fall. 

Apple/Screenshot by James Martin/CNET

Where there’s no comparison at all is with emergency features. The Apple Watch has emergency SOS, fall detection, satellite connectivity (on 5G models) and crash detection that automatically contacts emergency services and your chosen contacts if something goes wrong. 

It can also ping your phone, which may not seem like it’s health-related, but is certainly a mental health boon for me in the sense that it prevents me from losing my mind when I can’t find it.

## Battery life is a no-brainer

Battery life isn’t even a competition. While the Apple Watch struggled to make it a day and a half on a charge, the Whoop powered through the two-week mark as promised without breaking a sweat. That means I’m far more likely to wear it around the clock. My patchwork charging strategy with the Apple Watch regularly leaves me with a dead battery before bed — or worse, before a workout. Does exercise even count if it wasn’t tracked?

The Whoop doesn’t even have to be taken off to juice back up, since the puck holds its own charge and snaps on for wireless top-ups. Unless you’re wearing it in your thong, of course, in which case I truly hope it’s coming off between washes.

The fact that it doesn’t have to come off my wrist means I’m more consistent at tracking my sleep. Since there are no gaps in my sleep data, all other data tied to it is more reliable, including menstrual tracking (which uses basal body temperature during sleep to detect ovulation). I’ve been tracking my cycle for 10 years and know it well enough to say the Whoop has been spot-on with its estimates. The Apple Watch also tracks my menstrual cycle, but calculates ovulation retroactively if you’ve been consistent with sleep tracking (which is when it measures temperature changes). That consistency has been harder for me on the Apple Watch, so my ovulation estimates aren’t as accurate on the Apple watch. If you want a tracker you can truly set and forget about on both the notification and charging front, Whoop is your pick.

[image: applevswhoop | https://www.cnet.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/5ab48400-1190-49ac-9382-cd04fa2ae1b1.jpg?fit=1200,675]

The Whoop (left) is great for training-focused metrics, while the Apple Watch is more of a generalist. 

Vanessa Hand Orellana/CNET

## Apple Watch vs. Whoop: Bottom line

Despite being a longtime Apple Watch wearer, I’m not itching to take the Whoop off my wrist. It’s one of the few wearables I’ve worn for 14 consecutive days that hasn’t irritated my skin. I’d consider keeping both if it weren’t for Whoop’s subscription cost and my fear of financial commitment. Currently, you can get the One membership for $149 ($50 off).

The Whoop band has given me valuable insights about my training habits and flagged trends about my own body I hadn’t even put together myself — hey there, hormonal fatigue. The AI coach gets sharper the longer it knows you, which means I’m actually invested in sticking with it and following its advice. 

But realistically, I’m still in the thick of raising young kids while holding down a demanding job, and fitness has to take a back seat. Sticking with the Whoop would be like paying for a fancy gym membership and only using it twice a month. For anyone in a different stage of life looking to level up their fitness and optimize for peak performance (without real-time guidance), the Whoop is likely a worthy investment. I’ll join your ranks soon enough.

Maybe the fact that I’m paying for it would hold me accountable, and I’d find a way to prioritize the guidance more often? Or maybe our timing’s just off? For now, I’ll stick with the dependable friend, the Apple Watch, who doesn’t drop knowledge at every turn, but speaks my language and shows up when I need it — whether it’s pointing out I’m running late, or letting me dictate a text while wrangling a toddler. 

[image: Apple Watch vs. Oura Ring: The One Feature That Tipped the Scale | https://cdn.ex.co/transformations-account/production/bf6379df-047b-4e0a-b804-89ce1cc89281/667c88d4-4c0f-5f86-84dd-960ae93d3289/thumbnail-1080.webp]

[image: Vanessa Hand Orellana | https://www.cnet.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/97c79260-311c-45fb-884e-9ef324cb580e.png?w=64]

Vanessa Hand Orellana

Principal Writer

Vanessa is a lead writer at CNET, reviewing and writing about the latest smartwatches and fitness trackers. She joined the brand first as an on-camera reporter for CNET's Spanish-language site, then moved on to the English side to host and produce some of CNET's videos and YouTube series. When she's not testing out the latest health tech, you can catch her on a hike or trail run with her family.

# WHOOP vs Apple Watch: Is Screen-Free Fitness Tracking the Superior Choice?

Written by Stephen Sheehan, CPT, CNC [-> /author/stephensheehan]. Updated by Stephen Sheehan, CPT, CNC on September 29, 2026. Expert-Verified by Amanda Capritto, CPT, CES, CNC, CF-L1, CSNC [-> /author/amanda-capritto]. (Author bio paragraphs, repeated three times on the page, omitted.)

We test and review fitness products based on an independent, multi-point methodology. If you use our links to purchase something, we may earn a commission. [Read our disclosures -> https://www.garagegymreviews.com/disclosure]

[image: A side-by-side image of whoop vs apple watch on peoples' wrists | https://i.garagegymreviews.com/356/625/724/4/featured-comparison-whoop-5-vs-apple-watch-series-11.webp]

Although I have no plans to stop wearing my Apple Watch, I’ll be the first to admit that having a smartwatch that essentially acts as an extension of my iPhone can be distracting. While I can weather the notification storm and mostly stay focused, others may prefer screenless devices like the [Oura Ring -> https://www.garagegymreviews.com/oura-ring-review], Samsung Galaxy Ring, or WHOOP 5.0. 

Which side of the [fitness tracker vs smartwatch -> https://www.garagegymreviews.com/fitness-tracker-vs-smartwatch] line do you fall on? This WHOOP vs Apple Watch breakdown will give you perspective on the similarities and differences between two popular wearables that both offer excellent tracking capabilities and a high degree of customization. 

So, if you’re on the fence about whether WHOOP or Apple will help you best stay accountable, use this side-by-side comparison to weigh the pros and cons of going with a screenless strap or one of the top smartwatches. 

Editor’s Note: Apple recently released the Series 12 Watch. While we haven’t gotten our hands on it yet, we will be sure to update this piece when we get to test the brand’s latest model.

WHOOP offers a screenless way to get valuable insight on your health and fitness. The lightweight sensor band continuously monitors a variety of metrics, including heart rate variability (HRV), resting heart rate, and sleep data. Rather than paying for the device upfront, you must choose from three subscription plans that allow you to take advantage of its capabilities. It’s a great choice if you’re a data-driven user who prefers a simpler, distraction-free method of tracking.

Meanwhile, the Apple Watch remains one of the most popular [fitness trackers -> https://www.garagegymreviews.com/best-fitness-trackers] on the market because it combines a sharp aesthetic with excellent functionality. Featuring a bright, crisp OLED display, you can track your workouts, get insight on your sleep, and stay connected with real-time text and call notifications.

## WHOOP vs Apple Watch at a Glance

| | WHOOP 5.0 | Apple Watch Series 11

| Price | Device included with membership | Starts at $399

| Subscription | WHOOP One ($199/year); WHOOP Peak ($239/year); WHOOP Life ($359/year) | N/A

| Battery Life | 14+ days | Up to 24 hours

| Display | None | Always-on retina LTPO3 OLED; 42mm or 46mm

| Metrics Tracked | Heart rate, resting HR, HRV, respiratory rate, sleep stages/score, recovery, strain, steps, calories, skin temperature, SpO₂, VO₂ max and menstrual-cycle insights; stress and Healthspan require Peak | Heart rate, resting HR, HRV, ECG, blood oxygen, wrist temperature, respiratory rate, sleep stages/score, activity, steps, calories, GPS distance/pace, elevation, training load, noise, cycle/ovulation estimates, depth and water temperature

| Safety Features | No fall detection, Crash Detection or Emergency SOS; Peak and Life plans include Health Monitor alerts | Emergency SOS, Fall Detection, Crash Detection, noise monitoring and Backtrack

| Notifications | Haptic alarm and app-based health/coaching alerts | Calls, texts, email and app alerts; alarms plus heart-rate, rhythm, hypertension and other health notifications

| Water Resistance | IP68; up to 10 meters for two hours | Up to 50 meters

| Warranty | Lifetime warranty with an active membership | 1-year limited warranty

## WHOOP Company Overview

Founded in 2012 by Harvard University student-athlete Will Ahmed, along with John Capodilupo and Aurelian Nicolae, WHOOP has become one of the most recognizable brands in the fitness industry thanks to the support of many professional athletes and sports organizations like CrossFit, Major League Baseball, and the PGA Tour. 

The first WHOOP band was released in 2015, with several iterations coming in subsequent years. You can check out our full [WHOOP 4.0 review -> https://www.garagegymreviews.com/whoop-4-review] for our experience with one of the more recent versions. The latest model, the WHOOP 5.0, hit the market in May 2025, alongside the medical-grade WHOOP MG, which adds advanced hardware for ECG monitoring and daily blood pressure insights. 

Whoop 5.0

GGR Score

We test and review fitness products based on an independent, multi-point methodology.

4.25

[image: Whoop 5.0 | https://i.garagegymreviews.com/116/149/938/8/whoop-5.0.webp]

Whoop 5.0

- Continuous heart rate, HRV, sleep, and strain tracking
- 5 day battery life & on-wrist charging
- Multiple strap styles and colors

Save $70 on WHOOP 4.0, $40 on WHOOP 5.0, and $60 on WHOOP MG bundles [See Details -> https://www.garagegymreviews.com/go/whoop/]

[Check Price -> https://www.garagegymreviews.com/go/whoop/]

## Apple Company Overview

Synonymous with tech innovation, Apple broke into the smartwatch market in 2015. Since then, the company has followed a similar path with its other hallmark devices, adding new capabilities over the years with each release. 

Many GGR team members are longtime Apple Watch users—myself included. While I still utilize the Series 8, we’ll be showcasing the Series 11, which hit the market in September 2025. Although Apple recently discontinued selling this model on its official store in favor of the newly launched Series 12, you can still find it on third-party retailers like Amazon, Walmart, and Target.  

Apple Watch 11

GGR Score

We test and review fitness products based on an independent, multi-point methodology.

4.7

[image: Apple Watch Series 11 | https://i.garagegymreviews.com/227/867/076/7/the-apple-watch-series-11-2.webp]

Apple Watch Series 11

- Best for everyday health tracking
- Up to 24-hour battery life
- Advanced sleep insights
- Slim, durable design

[Check Price -> https://amzn.to/4c4QAOU]

## WHOOP vs Apple Watch: Key Similarities and Differences

Similarities

Both devices monitor key health metrics, including heart rate, calories burned, and blood oxygen levels

Both are meant to be worn around the wrist; though you can wear the WHOOP 5.0 around your biceps or in clothing from the brand’s WHOOP Body line.

You can select from a number of different band color and material options for either device.

Both the WHOOP and the Apple Watch can track more than 100 types of workouts.

Both devices offer sleep and cycle tracking.

Both have vibrating alarms and integrate seamlessly with third-party health and fitness services

Differences

The WHOOP 5.0 is a screenless device; the Apple Watch Series 11 features an OLED always-on retina display.

A WHOOP membership is required to access the device and its insights, with plans ranging from $199 to $359 per year. There is no fee to use the Apple Watch. However, there’s a higher upfront cost for the device itself. 

While the Apple Watch Series 11 has built-in GPS and can record routes without a phone, WHOOP relies on a connected phone for mapped routes.

The WHOOP WHOOPs the Apple Watch in terms of battery life, offering 14 days of usage compared to up to 24 hours of normal use or 38 hours in low-power mode. 

The Apple Watch Series 11 offers superior water resistance (50 meters) than the WHOOP 5.0 (up to 10 meters for two hours). 

Apple Watches allow you to receive and respond to calls, texts, and other notifications from your wrist. WHOOP devices do not.

RELATED: [WHOOP vs Oura -> https://www.garagegymreviews.com/whoop-vs-oura] and [Best Apple Watch -> https://www.garagegymreviews.com/best-apple-watch]

## Price

It would be unfair to make an apples-to-apples pricing comparison here because WHOOP and Apple market these devices very differently. 

### WHOOP

With WHOOP, you don’t actually pay for the band itself. Instead, you pay a membership fee that allows you to utilize all of its tracking capabilities and features. Here’s a breakdown of the three-tiered system: 

- WHOOP One: Costs $199 per year and includes the WHOOP 5.0 sensor, core recovery, strain, and sleep tracking.
- WHOOP Peak: Costs $239 per year and adds on health and stress monitors, plus longevity data.
- WHOOP Life: Costs $359 per year and includes the medical-grade WHOOP MG sensor, ECG heart screener, and blood pressure insights.

After you’ve completed a 12-month commitment, you can opt for monthly billing. That averages out to $25 per month for WHOOP One, $30 per month for WHOOP Peak, and $40 per month for WHOOP Life. 

[image: Whoop 5.0 on our tester's wrist | https://i.garagegymreviews.com/430/779/485/whoop-v5-on-the-wrist-of-our-tester-2.webp]

The Whoop 5.0

RELATED: [Best Budget Fitness Trackers -> https://www.garagegymreviews.com/best-budget-fitness-tracker]

### Apple Watch

On the other hand, the Apple Watch doesn’t have a subscription model. However, it does require a fairly hefty upfront cost, depending on which model you choose. 

As I mentioned earlier, the Series 11 is no longer available on the Apple store, but you can find it on third-party retailers starting at $399 for the 42mm model and $429 for the 46mm model. 

[image: Our tester wearing the Apple Watch Series 11 | https://i.garagegymreviews.com/178/380/644/7/our-tester-wearing-the-apple-watch-series-11-1.webp]

The Apple Watch Series 11

## Design and Comfort

Talk about two ends of the fitness tracker spectrum. On one hand, you have a screenless, more discreet device in WHOOP. On the other hand, you have a premium smartwatch with a fantastic touch screen. Here’s a more detailed breakdown of how each device is constructed and how it feels on your wrist. 

### WHOOP

Is the WHOOP 5.0 the most aesthetically pleasing fitness tracker? We’d be lying if we said yes. However, even though it doesn’t have a screen, it’s still well-built, lightweight, and available in a multitude of color options. In fact, WHOOP claims that there are 74,000 color and material combinations.

[image: Our tester holds an unlatched Whoop 5.0 | https://i.garagegymreviews.com/261/918/817/3/our-tester-holding-the-whoop-v5-1.webp]

Our tester holds an unlatched Whoop 5.0

The WHOOP 5.0 band comes in a variety of materials, including: 

- SuperKnit: Soft, flexible everyday band for all-day comfort and performance
- Meridian: Stylish woven band with a timeless design
- SportFlex: Durable silicone band made for workouts, movement, and easy cleaning
- Navigator: Rugged outdoor band designed to handle demanding activities and outdoor elements
- CoreKnit: Performance-focused knit band that combines comfort, durability, and flexibility

Although the company claims it “feels like nothing” on your wrist, GGR founder [Coop Mitchell -> https://www.garagegymreviews.com/author/coop] says, “I definitely notice it there, especially when working out and hitting it with a kettlebell or something, but it’s not much of a nuisance.” 

### Apple Watch

The Apple Watch Series 11 comes in two finishes: aluminum or titanium. The former starts at $399, while the latter starts at $699. 

[image: Our tester looking at metrics in the Apple Watch Series 11 | https://i.garagegymreviews.com/308/658/142/9/our-tester-wearing-the-apple-watch-series-11-3.webp]

The Apple Watch Series 11 on our tester’s wrist

You can also choose between a 42-millimeter or 46-millimeter case. Apple also gives you three standard band options: a flexible, swim-proof silicone rubber, a soft, lightweight textile, or a more sophisticated stainless steel. 

Although I’m several series behind, I love the look of my Apple Watch Series 8 with the standard black rubber band. If I was keen on fashion, I’d have a few other options to match whatever outfit I’m wearing. I also appreciate that you can purchase third-party bands, so you don’t have to go with the stock options from Apple. Overall, you can’t go wrong with a well-designed smartwatch that can be highly customized to your liking. 

## Battery Life and Charging

One of the main factors users look for in a fitness tracker is battery life. After all, you want your device to last long enough that you can get a ton done without needing to plug it back in. Who wins the battery life battle between WHOOP vs. Apple Watch? 

### WHOOP

One of the few areas where the WHOOP 5.0 stands head and shoulders above the Apple Watch is battery life. This device can stay powered on for 14 days—a remarkable feat for a fitness tracker. According to WHOOP, it takes about 120 minutes to fully charge the device.

In addition, WHOOP sells a waterproof wireless battery pack for $49 that allows you to fully charge your device as you’re wearing it in about two hours. That’s a super convenient feature that ensures you won’t run out of juice. 

### Apple Watch

The Apple Watch Series 11 has a battery life of up to 24 hours on normal use. According to Apple, it can last for 38 hours on low-power mode. This is solid, but not nearly as impressive as the WHOOP 5.0, which can last for a whopping two weeks. 

GGR expert product tester Kayla Godfrey is a longtime Apple Watch user, but she points out that the battery life is the biggest drawback, even with the Series 11. 

“I have had good luck with the 11 holding its battery, but my last watch would barely make it through the day and die,” she explains. “Typically I can get almost two full days of wearing my watch, but I charge it every night because it is a part of my routine.”

## Fitness and Workout Tracking

Obviously, this is what matters most when you’re investing hundreds of dollars on a piece of fitness technology. Both the WHOOP 5.0 and Apple Watch Series 11 stand out for their array of workout and health tracking features, so let’s dive into what each model can (and can’t) do. 

### WHOOP

The WHOOP 5.0 gives readings in four critical areas: sleep, recovery, strain, and stress. Of course, you must sync your strap to the WHOOP app to record your workouts—a minor annoyance if you expected your fitness tracker to automatically track everything you do. Thankfully, the app is available for both iOS and Android users.

[image: Overview of metrics in the Whoop app | https://i.garagegymreviews.com/233/654/683/7/whoop-app-screenshot-2.webp]

Overview of metrics in the Whoop app

What can you expect from the WHOOP app? You’ll be able to see graphs with your average heart rate data, max heart rate, HRV, and calories burned. This data is used to determine your workout strain (how hard you trained on a specific day). GGR expert product tester Sommer Fritz finds that part to be far more valuable than simply looking at her step count.

“Who cares if you’ve taken 10,000 steps if your heart rate never got out of zone 1?” she says. “The movement is helpful for your body, but I’m more focused on cardiovascular health, and the strain is a better measure of my workouts. I watch my heart rate throughout my workout and make sure I’m in the zone I desire.”

RELATED: [Understanding Your Target Heart Rate -> https://www.garagegymreviews.com/target-heart-rate]

So, what exactly can you track with the WHOOP 5.0? The device automatically detects more than 100 workout and activity types, including strength training, running, and cycling. The strain score ranges from 0 to 21, which can help you balance your workout intensity. Plus, the band even measures muscular load using volume and intensity. Both of these are reflected in your Strain and Recovery scores. This can help you know when it’s WHOOP can help you know when it’s time for a rest or [active recovery -> https://www.garagegymreviews.com/what-is-active-recovery] day. 

### Apple Watch

The main reason I got my Apple Watch was to keep track of my workouts. Years later, I still use it daily for this exact reason. Kayla relies on her Series 11 to help record her daily activity and stay on top of her routine. 

“With the ring graphics, I can easily see how consistent my movement has been through the week,” she explains. “There are some weeks when I haven’t logged a typical workout, however after looking at my watch, I can see I was active during work. I’m constantly lifting equipment, coaching kids’ sports teams, and moving throughout the day, and sometimes I forget how intensive my days truly are.” 

Similar to the WHOOP, the Apple Watch offers comprehensive fitness and workout tracking, including the ability to build custom workouts. Runners will appreciate how the built-in GPS delivers precise mapping and splits. Meanwhile, strength training enthusiasts will appreciate the training load technology that measures how the intensity and duration of your workouts impact your body over time. 

[image: Screenshots of workout data from the Apple Health app | https://i.garagegymreviews.com/477/427/126/apple-health-app-workout-data-screenshots.webp]

The Apple Health app records valuable metrics about your workouts

As for the accuracy of the data? [Research shows -> https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0353261] a margin of error up to 25% for calorie burn tracking1. However, if there’s a silver lining, the Apple Watch Series 8 performed better than the other three devices in the study (the Fitbit Sense 2, Samsung Galaxy Watch 5, and Garmin Forerunner 955). So, while it may not be the most accurate, it’s a step above many competitors. 

“Even with the calories projected, it seems in line with what I would be burning during a workout,” Kayla explains, “For example, during a 50-minute HIIT-style workout with 35 minutes of aggressive training, I burn 200 to 300 calories. That seems on par with the style of workouts I am doing.”

Finally, it’s worth mentioning that tracking your activity doesn’t have to be a one-person ordeal. In fact, this can be a great way for you and your friends to hold yourselves accountable. 

“I also share my workouts with a couple of my friends, so when I see they logged a workout, it’s a good reminder for me to also get at it,” Kayla says.

Fortunately for Apple Watch users, these devices are the kings of connectivity (as long as you have an iPhone). Not only can you keep track of all of your data in the Apple Fitness and Apple Health apps, but you can download a number of third-party apps to take full advantage of the tracking technology.

## Sleep Tracking

Monitoring your heart rate and calorie expenditure can be quite valuable. However, that’s not the only reason to invest in a fitness tracker. Recovery is perhaps the most underappreciated component of a balanced wellness routine, and both the WHOOP 5.0 and Apple Watch Series 11 offer advanced sleep tracking capabilities, too. 

### WHOOP

The WHOOP 5.0 automatically records a number of key sleep metrics, including: 

- Sleep stages: Divides your night into Awake, Light, Deep, and REM sleep
- Sleep performance: How many hours your slept vs. your calculated physiological sleep need
- Sleep efficiency: The percentage of time you spent actually sleeping
- Sleep consistency: How closely your recent bedtimes and wake times align with your circadian rhythm

WHOOP can help you schedule your bed and wake times based on how challenging your day was, when you need to wake up, and what your workout will be the following day. Plus, this sleep data can help you be more aware of your overall health. 

“I can usually predict when I’m getting sick just by watching my sleep, temperature, and recovery numbers,” Sommer explains. “It helps me to up my water, supplements, and sleep time to head off a virus.” 

[image: Sleep analytics in the Whoop app | https://i.garagegymreviews.com/460/870/610/screenshot-from-the-whoop-app-3.webp]

Sleep analytics in the Whoop app

Overall, WHOOP’s biggest advantage is the way it connects sleep to recovery. Overnight heart-rate variability, resting heart rate, respiratory rate, and sleep data feed into the daily Recovery score, while the Journal can help identify how behaviors such as alcohol, caffeine, stress, or late meals correlate with sleep and recovery.

“I really like how the health monitoring shows me how alcohol and other factors affect my body,” Sommer says. “This is motivating me to stay on the straight and narrow.”

### Apple Watch

The Apple Watch Series 11 can also provide valuable sleep insights. It estimates total sleep and time spent awake or in Core, Deep, and REM sleep. You can view nightly results or long-term trends in the Sleep and Health apps (another plus for connectivity). 

Your Sleep Score is calculated on a 0-100 scale based on sleep duration, bedtime consistency, and nighttime interruptions. This can give you good context about whether you had a restful night or whether you need to improve your sleep hygiene habits. 

Of course, you don’t have to utilize the Apple Watch for its sleep tracking capabilities. 

“I wanted something that tracked my activity level, but didn’t want to get into the weeds of sleep and recovery like WHOOP,” Kayla explains. “I think Apple does a good job of tracking things like sleep, but I don’t need a device harassing me about things like recovery.” 

## Smartwatch Features

Obviously, WHOOP focuses on activity and sleep tracking, but without a screen, it doesn’t offer as much functionality as the Apple Watch. 

The latter brings connectivity to the forefront, essentially acting as an extension of your iPhone. 

“I like how not only I can track my fitness, but I can also keep all my devices synced together,” Kayla says. “Having my watch allows me to track my activity level, keep up with my important notifications, and also ping my phone when I lose it for the eighth time that day.” 

While I don’t lose my phone that many times on a daily basis, I echo Kayla’s sentiment about the synchronicity factor. It’s quite convenient to be able to quickly check an e-mail or respond to a text message from my wrist without having to pull out my phone. 

Here are some other key smartwatch capabilities you can take advantage of with the Series 11: 

- Safety and location features: Includes Emergency SOS, Fall Detection, Crash Detection, Check in, Find My, and Compass Backtrack for retracing your route. 
- Mobile payments: Leave your credit card at home and use Apple Pay for seamless transactions.
- Notifications: Receive and respond to texts, calls, emails, calendar alerts, and app notifications right from your wrist.

Personally, I love how convenient it is to check into my local gym by just tapping my watch on the scanner or paying for my groceries without pulling out my wallet. While I have a bit of a love-hate relationship with real-time notifications (sometimes it’s nice to disconnect), the Apple Watch has the versatility advantage over the WHOOP 5.0. 

## Additional Features

But wait, there’s more! 

Let’s touch upon a few other notable features that may affect your purchasing decision. 

### Water Resistance

While the WHOOP 5.0 is “waterproof,” it wasn’t designed for deep sea diving or anything of the like. It only goes up to 10 meters (32 feet), a far cry from the Apple Watch, which can be submerged up to 50 meters (164 feet).

### Cycle Tracking

Women can utilize these devices for cycle support. Here’s an explanation of how each one works: 

#### WHOOP

According to WHOOP, their Menstrual Cycle Insights can: 

- Log cycle phases and correlate with metrics like skin temperature and your Recovery Score
- Track symptoms and display patterns across cycle phases
- Anticipate potential symptoms based on your physiology and past logs
- Predict possible period start, which can help inform your training and recovery
- Overlay phases on trends such as Recovery, Sleep, and Strain metrics
- Provide personalized insights on how hormonal shifts affect your performance, mood, and energy levels

In addition, WHOOP offers Pregnancy Insights that include personalized coaching, symptom tracking, and biometric integration. Plus, they offer a free year-long subscription to Natural Cycles through their new partnership. While you should still work with your healthcare provider, using the device can certainly help you make better-informed decisions. 

RELATED: [Exercise During Pregnancy -> https://www.garagegymreviews.com/exercise-during-pregnancy]

#### Apple

Apple’s Cycle Tracking app lets users record menstrual flow, spotting, symptoms, pregnancy, lactation, and contraceptive use. It uses logged information and heart-rate data to predict upcoming periods and fertile windows. 

According to Apple, your watch also uses overnight wrist temperature data to provide retrospective ovulation estimates and improve future period predictions. Overall, the Apple Watch is great for menstrual and ovulation tracking, but the WHOOP provides more insight into how your cycle affects your workouts, recovery, stress, and sleep.  

[image: Our tester looking at metrics in the Apple Watch Series 11 | https://i.garagegymreviews.com/352/070/157/4/our-tester-wearing-the-apple-watch-series-11-2.webp]

Our tester looking at fitness metrics in the Apple Watch Series 11

## Company Policies

From warranties to returns to customer service, these little details can make a huge impact on your purchasing experience. Luckily, both WHOOP and Apple rate highly in this area. 

### WHOOP

WHOOP covers the device against material and workmanship defects for life, as long as you maintain an active membership. In addition, you can try the WHOOP 5.0 for 30 days from the date of delivery before deciding whether you want to return it. You will have to pay for shipping and handling in order to receive a full refund. 

### Apple

Apple isn’t quite so generous, as it only provides a one-year limited warranty. However, you can get added peace of mind and protection with the affordable AppleCare+ program. At just $4.99 per month or $79 for two years for the Series 11 or 12, this protection plan extends your coverage and includes unlimited incidents of accidental damage protection. You can also finance your Apple Watch with an Apple Card, which gives 3% daily cash back upfront on the full cost of your Apple Watch. 

## Which Fitness Tracker Should You Choose?

As a certified personal trainer and lifelong athlete, I’m all about taking advantage of tools that can help you raise your health and fitness game to a new level. That being said, there are distinct differences between these devices that may make one a better choice than the other. 

### Choose WHOOP if:

- You don’t want to be distracted by a screen or phone notifications
- You’re an athlete who wants in-depth sleep and recovery data
- You want maximum battery life for continuous use 

### Choose Apple if:

- You want to remain connected to answer calls and texts
- You’re a runner who needs GPS tracking capabilities
- You want a stylish, sleek smartwatch that can be customized to match your aesthetic

[image: Screenshot showing steps data from the Apple Health app | https://i.garagegymreviews.com/126/074/835/4/apple-health-app-steps-data-screenshots.webp]

The Apple Watch is excellent at tracking steps, which you can also track in the Apple Health app

## Final Thoughts

Is WHOOP worth the hype? If you’re less worried about staying in the loop with all your calls, emails, and texts and more focused on getting insight into your health, recovery, and sleep, it’s a solid option. Plus, we like that you aren’t tied down to wearing this gadget around your wrist, as WHOOP’s Body line makes it possible to keep this tracker hidden in a sports bra, leggings, jacket, and other compatible apparel. 

However, the Apple Watch remains one of the best fitness trackers because it checks so many boxes beyond tracking your workouts and sleep. It functions well with a variety of third-party apps and fits seamlessly into the ever-expanding Apple ecosystem. So, if you’re an iPhone user looking to level up your health and fitness in style, it’s hard to go wrong with any of the Apple Watch models on the market. 

Ultimately, you need to decide whether a screenless (aka distraction-free) device that requires a monthly subscription is a better investment than a smartwatch with a higher upfront cost that keeps you connected at all times.

## FAQs

### What are the main differences between the WHOOP and Apple Watch?

WHOOP emphasizes recovery, sleep, and training strain through a subscription, while Apple Watch offers broader workout, health, smartwatch, and app features with a screen and no subscription cost.

### What are some of the best fitness tracker brands?

While the GGR team has been impressed by Apple and WHOOP, we’ve also enjoyed our tracking experiences with Fitbit, Garmin, and Oura. Each brand offers a variety of devices, so check out our individual reviews and roundups for more insight.

### Is WHOOP actually worth it?

The Garage Gym Reviews team believes the WHOOP 5.0 is only worth it if you’re a serious athlete looking for in-depth health and sleep data. Look elsewhere if you want a more versatile device, especially if you want a more traditional smartwatch with a display.
